The founder's numbers are pinned to the launch era (the founder's gap-11 rule): the YC company page as captured on
2025-10-16, the partnership terms page of 2025-10-15 and the Launch YC post of 2025-10-19. Anything later is under
*Status today*.

  https://www.codyco.ai/

## The founder-emulation items

1. **Who (practitioner `agent`).** YC-C names hotel groups with "call centers and central reservation departments";
   YC-L's video features front-desk staff at a Munich hotel. *My choice:* the reservation agent, central office or
   front desk, who sees the missed-call list. Segment: hotel groups in Germany with a central office or call center.
2. **When (circumstance, occasion, window).** YC-L's "After hours. During peak hours. On holidays." *My choice:* the
   occasion "reservation shift", window the last 7 days (calls come in on every shift; spec 120's "every shift" -> 7
   DAYS), Frequency 5 to 7 days out of 7.
3. **Who pays (decision-maker `director`, Buyer and payer, Purchase friction).** TERMS addresses the hotel group;
   YC-L asks to "book a 10-minute call if you lead a hotel group". *My choice:* the revenue or reservations director
   decides, the hotel's owner has to agree. Purchase friction tests "A data protection review of guest calls" (German
   hotels handle guests' card and personal data on the call); my choice, no source names it.
4. **Mechanism.** YC-C: missed calls forwarded to Codyco, the AI answers, bookings appear in the PMS. Compatibility
   tests call forwarding (the mechanism needs it); Adoption friction tests letting the AI answer in the hotel's voice.
5. **Cost, price, ability.** As in the table. Reading `budget` by the engine (a percent of calls against euros).
6. **Commitment.** TERMS and YC-L: the paid, money-back pilot at one location. The step carries its number ("pay
   €3,000 for a money-back pilot at one hotel"), the gap-8 check.

## The respondents

No first-person account by a German reservation agent or revenue director was found in public (no HN thread; the
site's quotes are curated testimonials). **Every person is the author's invention**, no real person's name is used,
and each is built on the public facts named here.

Reservation agents (Parts 1 and 2):
- Lena Hoffmann: a trade-fair Saturday in a Munich central office; built on YC-L ("During peak hours") and the Munich
  hotel YC-L features.
- Murat Yilmaz: a check-in rush at the desk; YC-L's "peak hours".
- Chiara Russo: a group whose call center already answers after hours (YC-C: "Even with call centers..."); her pain is
  group emails, so Importance and Current solution go against the founder.
- Jonas Weber: alone on a Sunday desk; YC-L's "On holidays" / after hours.
- Aylin Demir: an old phone system that cannot forward (Compatibility only_with_help); the author's.
- Tobias Brandl: the sceptic who will not hand guests to an AI (Relative advantage negative, Adoption no); the author's.
- Elif Kaya: weekend abandoned calls seen on Monday; YC-L's "After hours".
- Daniel Okonkwo: rates pushed wrong to agencies matter more (Importance against); the author's.
- Mehmet Arslan: a vague story, GUESSED. Katarina Novak: a story chip, GUESSED.
- Florian Gruber, Nadia Haddad: gate No (no unanswered booking call in the 7 days).

Revenue directors (COMMERCIAL_B2B link, Part 3): Stefanie Wagner (6%), Andreas Keller (4%, below the founder's 5%),
Roberto Bianchi (8%), Ingrid Lindholm (2%, a call center covers after hours), Karim Benali (does not know his rate;
YC-L's "Free AI Strategy Workshop" and SITE's free test number as his ask), Petra Vogel (5%), Hannes Moser (nothing,
would not pay), Joanna Wiśniewska (10% at resort hotels in high season). The value boxes are percents of the calls, in
the founder's unit and period; the price picks are two codes, the pilot's rung and the licence's rung, each placed
against the founder's €3,000 and €1,000.

## Status today

Same idea (SITE, 2026-10-22): "Turn missed hotel calls into paid bookings.", widened to payments, invoices and
handovers; "Running at 15+ hotel groups" (the launch said 7); "€10k+ bookings written directly into the PMS". **No
public price today** (SITE and /faq show none); the €3,000 pilot terms remain the only priced source.

## Open (what could not be sourced, and the workarounds)

- **The licence amount** was never public. €1,000 to €1,500 per hotel a month is the operator's reading of the pilot's
  monthly rate (above). Treat the plan step's reading as a reading of that derivation.
- **Dollars or euros.** YC-L says "$5,000", YC-C "€5,000" for the same hotel; the pilot fee is in euros and the company
  is in Munich, so the entry is in euros. The market is DE, and the golden corpus's rule U (US only) is a note.
- **The "> 8 hotels" / "10 hotels" roll-out threshold** in TERMS and YC-L disagree; the entry does not use it.
- **Job titles.** Neither the agent nor the director is named in public; both are my choices (items 1 and 3).
- **The 5% is the founders' claim** for "the best" offices; no independent figure was sought.
- **UPFRONT_THEN has no "credited" or "money-back" flag**; the fee is a plain up-front amount (header).

whys.g1: Karim and Ingrid both want to see the missed calls on their own numbers before paying, so they belong together under a plain name, while Hannes's outright refusal and Andreas's sum that the licence costs more than it brings in are different reasons and rightly stand alone.
whys.g2: There is no junk, explicit or off-topic answer on this line; all four answers speak to price and what the tool would be worth.

founder.asked_twice: Screens 20 and 22: I name the paid pilot at one hotel as the first real step on 20, then 'Offer a pilot?' asks about it again on 22.

screens.why2: Data protection review, PMS and a trial at one hotel are all words I use every day with hotel groups, and the short intro is clear on first reading.
screens.why3: I sell to hotel groups and know from my pilot talks that these steps come up before they buy, so I can judge the list without guessing.
screens.why4: The three rows are distinct and in my buyers' words, covering the guest-data review, the PMS check and the one-hotel trial that matches my pilot, and I can edit them if one is missing.
screens.why5: The data protection review and one-hotel trial are mine, but the belief's 'about 4 weeks' is a limit my material does not give, so it drifts slightly from what I typed.
screens.instead: Keep the three rows and ask: How long can a data protection review of guest calls take before the deal is at risk: 2 weeks, 4 weeks, 8 weeks, or longer?

screens.why1: Right after naming what could slow a purchase, it is obvious why I pick the one step to test and say how long I expect it to take.
screens.why2: I can answer it, and DPA review and PMS are my daily words, but 'how long would this step take before it went through' needs a second read and the hint is printed twice.
screens.why3: From selling to hotel groups in Germany, I can pick the likeliest blocker and put a number of weeks on it, and an estimate is all the screen asks for.
screens.why4: The three steps are distinct, the units fit and the review and PMS check are real hurdles, but 'a trial at one hotel first' is my own up-to-8-week pilot rather than a step that 'goes through', so it sits oddly here.
screens.why5: The belief keeps my data protection review of guest calls and my 4 weeks, and 'or not need it' fairly covers groups that have no such review.
screens.instead: Which step could hold up the purchase most? A data protection review of guest calls / A check that bookings land in our PMS / A trial at one hotel first. How long do you expect it to take from start to sign-off? [number] [days, weeks, months]

screens.why1: After who decides, cost, price and what could stop a purchase, asking what first real step I'd want from the director is the obvious last commercial question, and my pilot is exactly that.
screens.why2: The question and its hint (time, data, money or a signature) are plain on first reading, and I can answer in my own words within 25 words.
screens.why3: The first step is what I actually ask hotel groups for, since my own terms set it as the €3,000 money-back pilot at one location.
screens.why4: The only chip is the escape, Leave this out of the study, which fits an optional test and sits cleanly beside the free-text box.
screens.why5: The belief keeps my €3,000, money-back pilot and one hotel exactly as I typed them, and the revenue director is the buyer I named; its "In most cases" and "now" are only Keel's framing of the claim.

screens.why1: Right after I named the first real step, it makes sense for Keel to show me how it wrote that step and what it will test before I save it.
screens.why2: The belief and the bar are plain to me, but the intro promises my step in under 9 words while the only wording shown runs to 19, so I have to read it twice to see which text it means.
screens.why3: The €3,000 money-back pilot at one location is my own offer, and I sell it to these directors, so I can check this line from what I know.
screens.why4: The screen shows a line to check and a test, with no options, rows, chips or value box to judge.
screens.why5: It keeps my step, €3,000 for a money-back pilot at one hotel, and the buyer I named; leaving out the credit on roll-out does not change what it means.
screens.instead: Your step as strangers hear it, under 9 words: Pay €3,000 for a money-back hotel pilot.

screens.why1: A last choice before the study goes out makes sense, but I named my €3,000 pilot as the first real step moments ago, so being asked whether to offer a pilot feels partly repeated.
screens.why2: "Pilot" is the word I use for my own offer, and the question and hint can be understood on first reading.
screens.why3: Whether to ask strangers for a pilot at the end of the study is my decision, and I know I want to.
screens.why4: "Yes, ask them" and "No pilot" are the only two answers, they are distinct and clear, and no escape chip is needed.
screens.why5: My pilot is paying €3,000 for a money-back pilot at one hotel, but the quoted line only says "Would you try this for real? Leave your email", so it drops the price, the money-back terms and the single hotel, and an email could pass for a yes to the paid pilot.
screens.instead: Offer your pilot at the end? People who say yes see: "Would you pay €3,000 for a money-back pilot at one hotel? Leave your email." Options: Yes, ask them / No pilot

screens.why1: Just before people see the study, choosing who asks my questions is an obvious last setup step, right after the pilot offer.
screens.why2: The question and voice choice are clear on first read, but the hint packs in video, typing, credits and text links, and 'records the voice' is odd when the interviewer also appears on video, so I need a second read to know whether I am picking a face or a voice.
screens.why3: I can listen to both samples and decide which one I want my reservation agents to hear, with no outside knowledge needed.
screens.why4: Two named interviewers with a five-second sample each are distinct and complete for this choice, and Daphne being preselected means I need not do anything; no escape is needed.
screens.why5: It says 'reservation agents', my own people, and changes nothing of what I typed about Codyco; the preselected interviewer is what I chose to keep.

screens.why1: Right after choosing how directors answer, the obvious last step before sending is deciding who receives the link.
screens.why2: The question and all three options read plainly on first pass, though 'the Contacts page' assumes I know that part of Keel.
screens.why3: I know exactly who I would reach, since I already have hotel group directors from my own network and the 7 groups we work with.
screens.why4: The three routes are distinct and cover how I would reach people, but there is no way to combine them, and I would likely mix named contacts with a Keel search.
screens.why5: My pick of people I know by name is kept as sending each person their own link, and nothing distorts my study.
screens.instead: Who gets a link? (pick any that apply): People I know by name, each with their own link / People I found with Keel, from a list on the Contacts page / A group, with one open link I post where they already are

screens.why_b1: The verdict and a number are on top, but the number is one card's (Existing sacrifice, 4 of 7), and 'People disagree' sits awkwardly with the footer's 'the worst of all its cards' when Purchase friction says Did not hold.
screens.why_b2: There is no chart here, but each card's count and bar are plain; I need a second look at why Existing sacrifice counts 7 when 8 answered, and at what '5 needed' means on Ability to pay.
screens.why_b3: The dimension names and belief lines are the ones I checked, word for word on Buyer and payer, Purchase friction and Commitment, with my €3,000 pilot and my 5%.
screens.why_b4: Nothing tells me what to do: the only statement explains who was asked, not whether to change the price, prepare for the data protection review or go ahead with the pilot sales.
screens.why_b5: No claim goes beyond the 8: the counts stay visible, the two held beliefs are marked 'at the bar' rather than strong, and Ability to pay is called too few to call.
screens.instead: Did not hold: 4 of 8 directors expect the data protection review to take longer than 4 weeks (bar: no more than 2), so prepare the review pack before selling, even though 6 of 8 would pay for the €3,000 pilot; the 4 of 8 on price is a split, and 8 people is a small sample.

screens.why_b1: "People disagree" sits directly above "4 of 7 lose 5% or more... bar 5 of 7 · 1 short", so I have both the verdict and the number that decides it.
screens.why_b2: The unit, the 7 people and the bar are all there, but the 5% on the axis and the bar of 5 of 7 people sit together as two different fives, so I need a second look to separate the marker from my 5%.
screens.why_b3: It is my 5% of reservation calls lost after hours, at peak or on a holiday, and although "Existing sacrifice" is Keel's label, I recognise the line as the belief I checked.
screens.why_b4: The So line repeats the count and points me to the Price card, without saying what a 4-to-3 split means for my 5% claim or my pitch to directors.
screens.why_b5: It stays with the people who answered, says "a small group: a lean, not a call", and shows that Hannes was counted as 0 and Karim was left out.
screens.instead: 4 of 7 lose 5% or more, 1 short of your bar, and the 3 below lose 4%, 2% and none, so don't lead with 5% as true for every group: find out what separates the two sides, then see on the Price card whether they would pay anyway.

screens.why_b1: "People disagree" sits directly above its deciding numbers: 4 of 8 at my price on each part, against a bar of 6 of 8, so 2 short.
screens.why_b2: The up-front chart reads at once, but the monthly chart and its strip add up to only 7 people under a bar of 6 of 8 and a verdict of 4 of 8, so I need a second look to see that Hannes, who would not pay at all, is missing from them.
screens.why_b3: The card is called Price and states my numbers as I hold them: €3,000 up front, then €1,000 per hotel a month, judged by hotel group revenue directors.
screens.why_b4: The So line gives the shortfall and points me to the Insights tab, but it does not say what this means for my €3,000 and €1,000, such as whether to test a lower price or narrow to the groups that accept it.
screens.why_b5: The n stays visible and the screen says "a small group: a lean, not a call", but the So line's "would pay your price" softly overstates answers to a question about what Codyco would be worth.
screens.instead: 4 of 8 said Codyco is worth €3,000 up front and €1,000 a month, 2 short of the bar, and this small group is only a lean: 3 put it lower and 1 would not pay at all (so the monthly chart shows 7), so before changing the price, see on Insights what separates the 4 who reached it from the 4 who did not.

screens.why_b1: "Too few to call" sits directly above its deciding number, 4 of 8 named my price or more with 5 needed, so I know this belief is not called and why.
screens.why_b2: The answers, the four people counted and the 3-of-4 bar are plain, but it takes a second look to see why a bar that looks met still gives "too few to call" and what the fifth, empty cell in the strip is.
screens.why_b3: My €3,000 and €1,000 and my hotel group revenue directors are there, but Ability to pay and this line are not among the beliefs I remember checking, so I recognise it from my price rather than as my own wording.
screens.why_b4: The So line says concretely that Price decides this stage and that this belief cannot be read until at least 5 name my price, so I know to deal with the price first.
screens.why_b5: Nothing is claimed beyond the people who answered: the 4 answers and the 4 not asked are visible, the small group is called "a lean, not a call", and the three budget-line answers are not called a pass.
screens.instead: Say why 5 is needed here when Price's bar is 6 of 8, and say that the 3 of 4 from a budget line is promising but does not count until 5 people name my price.

screens.why_b1: Holding up sits directly beside 6 of 8 against a bar of 6 of 8, so I can see the belief held, and only just, at the bar.
screens.why_b2: The four answers are drawn with their counts and marked for or against, the 8 people are plain, and the marker sits at 6, all on first look.
screens.why_b3: Buyer and payer and the line about the revenue director deciding with the hotel's owner agreeing are exactly what I checked on the way in.
screens.why_b4: Plan for the owner tells me concretely to bring the owner into my sales process and not to expect the director to sign alone, though 2 of 8 can.
screens.why_b5: The count line says this is a small group and a lean, not a call, but 'the hotel's owner in most deals' is a soft overstatement because only 4 of 8 named the owner, which is half.
screens.instead: Plan for a second signature in most deals: 4 of 8 need the hotel's owner, 2 need someone else or several people, and 2 could sign alone.

screens.why_b1: "Did not hold" sits right beside its deciding number, 4 of 8 expect longer than 4 weeks against a bar of no more than 2 of 8, so I know the answer and why.
screens.why_b2: The bands, the 8 people and the for and against marks are plain, but I need a second look to match the chart's bar of 6 of 8 to the headline's no more than 2 of 8, and to see why the band starting at my own 4 weeks counts against me.
screens.why_b3: The card's name and belief line are the ones I checked, word for word, although the fragment "You said a data protection review of guest calls" reads oddly.
screens.why_b4: It tells me concretely to plan for a review cycle of 4 weeks to 3 months and points me to the Insights tab for what would take the time.
screens.why_b5: n is visible and the small group is called a lean, but the flat "Did not hold" and "longer than your 4 weeks" lean a little hard on four people whose band begins at exactly my 4 weeks, so some may be nearer my figure than the line implies.
screens.instead: Did not hold, on a small group: 4 of 8 picked 4 weeks to 3 months and 4 expect less or no review, against a bar of no more than 2 of 8 picking that band or longer, so plan for a review that may run past 4 weeks; the band starts at my 4 weeks, so this does not show how far past.

screens.why_b1: The verdict 'Holding up' sits directly beside '6 of 8 said yes, bar 6 of 8, at the bar', so I can see that my belief held and that it only just cleared the bar.
screens.why_b2: On first look I can see it counts answers to the €3,000 pilot question across 8 directors (6 yes, 1 probably not, 1 no), with my bar marked at 6 of 8.
screens.why_b3: The card's name and belief line are word for word the Commitment belief I checked, including the €3,000 money-back pilot at one hotel.
screens.why_b4: 'Book them into it' tells me exactly what to do next: put the six directors who said yes into the paid pilot.
screens.why_b5: The small group is stated and n stays visible, but 'would pay' and 'Book them into it' treat a hypothetical yes as ready to book at exactly the bar, without noting that only 4 of 8 named €3,000 or more on Price.
screens.instead: 6 of 8 say they would pay €3,000, exactly at your bar, but that is a small group answering a hypothetical and only 4 of 8 named €3,000 or more on Price, so ask the six to book the pilot now and see who actually pays.

screens.why_b1: Every box puts its verdict beside the number that decides it, such as Price at 4 of 8 against a bar of 6, Purchase friction at 4 of 8 against no more than 2, and Buyer and payer at 6 of 8 at the bar.
screens.why_b3: The dimension names and belief lines are the ones I checked, down to the €3,000 up front, the €1,000 per hotel a month, the 4-week data protection review, and the director deciding with the owner agreeing.
screens.why_b4: The screen never says what these results mean for my idea, so I have to work out for myself that I should offer a test on their own call numbers, and the failed Purchase friction line gives me nothing to act on.
screens.why_b5: Nothing goes beyond who answered: the counts stay visible, each quote is named, the two-person groups show their size, and the screen openly says that nobody was asked why on Purchase friction and names the 4 who never saw the question.
screens.why_b6: The quotes add what I did not type: Karim's phone system can't show his missed share, Ingrid wants missed bookings on her own numbers, Andreas's 4% across nine hotels doesn't cover the licence, and Joanna's MD signed off a tool after seeing it run at one hotel.
screens.instead: Price splits on proof: two want to see their own missed calls before paying, and at 4% the licence does not pay across nine hotels, so offer a call-count test before the €3,000 pilot; 4 of 8 expect the data protection review to run past 4 weeks but nobody was asked why, so ask them what would take the time.

screens.why1: As the first screen of a study about my work, it makes sense to check straight away whether my hotel group has the setup the study is about.
screens.why2: Central reservations office and call center are everyday words in my trade, and I can answer on first reading.
screens.why3: As revenue director, I know exactly how our group handles reservations.
screens.why4: Yes and No cover the factual question without overlap, and the gate rightly has no escape chip.
screens.why5: Nothing about a product, a founder's idea or anyone's role leaks; it only asks about how my group is set up.
screens.why6: Heard once, it is one short question with an obvious yes-or-no answer and nothing that only the eye can read.

screens.why1: Straight after the question about our central reservations office, it is obvious why I am shown the idea before being asked what I would pay or how buying it would go.
screens.why2: PMS, OPERA Cloud, Sihot, Apaleo, forwarding calls and handing to the desk are everyday words in my job, so I understand it on first reading.
screens.why3: Unanswered booking calls, our PMS and the rules for what reaches our reservations desk are things I know and decide on directly.
screens.why4: This is a card to read, with no options, chips or value box.
screens.why5: It is a deliberately shown idea card in terms my trade uses, with no internal role labels or study jargon reaching me.
screens.why6: It says well in short sentences with no parenthesis or slash, but six sentences is a lot to hold from one hearing, and the list "your PMS, OPERA Cloud, Sihot or Apaleo" is a small mouthful when heard.

screens.why1: Right after an idea about answering booking calls, it makes obvious sense to ask how many of those calls my group loses today.
screens.why2: I know the term, but "lost" could mean abandoned and unanswered calls or answered calls that did not book, and I would pause to decide which one is meant.
screens.why3: I see our call center reports and can give a figure from memory, about 6% for our group.
screens.why4: A percent box suits the question, and None and I can't recall are distinct and cover the honest answers that are not a number.
screens.why5: Nothing of the founder's product or role terms leaks, and "reservation calls" and "lost" are words my trade uses.
screens.why6: The question says well once, but "or a low and a high; none is 0" is clipped instruction-speak that I would need to hear twice.
screens.instead: Last month, about what percent of your group's reservation calls went unanswered? Say a percent, or a low and a high. If none, say none. Or say you can't recall.

screens.why1: I've just said what share of calls we lose and seen the idea, so it's obvious why I'm now being asked what it would be worth to me per hotel.
screens.why2: The question and 'per hotel' are clear at once, but in my trade an 'agent' is a person on my reservations team, so 'an agent for unanswered calls' above it makes me stop and check that this means software.
screens.why3: I buy tools like this per property and know what lost bookings and our call center cost, so I can put a number on it from my own budget.
screens.why4: The bands are distinct and cover the range and 'I can't say' fits, but on the up-front step 'I wouldn't pay for this' merges 'I'd pay monthly but no setup fee' with rejecting it outright, and that first answer is a common one for me.
screens.why5: The card is shown on purpose and nothing of the founder's plan or internal terms reaches me beyond the idea and a plain two-part price.
screens.why6: Each step is one short question with four amounts I can hold and a clean two-band follow-up, and 'Or say you can't say' is only slightly clumsy.
screens.instead: Imagine Codyco, an AI that answers the calls your team misses. What would it be worth to you up front, per hotel? Nothing up front, I'd only pay monthly · Under €1,000 · €1,000 to under €3,000 · €3,000 to under €5,000 · €5,000 to under €10,000 · €10,000 or more · I wouldn't pay for this at all

screens.why1: Right after I named a price, it makes sense to ask where the money for it would come from.
screens.why2: Budget line, signed off and up front are everyday words in my job, and the amounts I gave are repeated back, so I can answer on first reading.
screens.why3: I hold the budget for booking tools at our group, so I know whether this would come from an existing line, a new one or another cost centre.
screens.why4: The four cover the real cases and the escape fits, but the options are in the past tense for a would-be purchase, and "There was no budget for it" isn't a source of money.
screens.why5: It only plays back my own figures and shows nothing new of the founder's product, plan or terms, though it doesn't repeat that the up-front amount was per hotel.
screens.why6: It is one short question with four short options I can hold after one hearing, and "Or say you can't say" and the tense shift are slightly clumsy but don't stop me answering.
screens.instead: You said about €3,000 to €5,000 up front, then €1,000 to €2,500 a month. If you went ahead at that, where would the money come from? A budget line we already have; a new budget line someone would sign off; taken from other spending; or there would be no budget for it. Escape: I can't say.

screens.why1: Right after asking where the money would come from, it makes sense to ask whether I could approve the spend myself.
screens.why2: "Sign off" is plain to me, but "the hotel's owner" fits one property better than a group, where approval would come from our managing director or CFO.
screens.why3: I know my own approval limit and who has to agree above it, so I can answer from how we actually buy tools.
screens.why4: My true answer fits, but "I can't recall one" makes no sense for a question about my authority, and "several people" can overlap with "someone else's decision" or the owner.
screens.why5: No product name, plan or founder's term for people reaches me, and the €3,000 comes from the price I just gave.
screens.why6: It is short and the four options can be held, but three start with "no", so they blur when heard, and "or say you can't recall one" sounds odd because nothing says what "one" is.
screens.instead: Could you sign off on about €3,000 per hotel yourself, or would someone else have to agree? Yes, I could sign off myself · No, group management would have to agree · No, the hotel's owner would have to agree · No, several people would have to agree · I can't say

screens.why1: Right after asking whether I could sign off myself, it makes sense to ask what else stands in the way, and in Germany a data protection review of guest calls is the obvious hurdle.
screens.why2: Data protection review is everyday language for anyone buying hotel systems in Germany, and I understand the question on first reading.
screens.why3: I've taken booking and guest-data tools through our data protection officer, so I can place how long a review of guest calls would take, even though it's an estimate.
screens.why4: The bands cover everything and the escape fits, but exactly 3 months fits both '4 weeks to 3 months' and '3 to 6 months', and exactly 6 months fits both '3 to 6 months' and 'Over 6 months'.
screens.why5: Codyco is the name from the idea card I was shown, and the step is one I'd recognise, with no founder's terms or internal roles reaching me.
screens.why6: It is one short question, with four options I can hold and one escape said last, and the second step is a simple either-or, so I could answer after hearing it once.
screens.instead: If you bought Codyco, how long would a data protection review of guest calls take before it went through? Under 2 weeks · 2 to under 4 weeks · 4 weeks to under 3 months · 3 to under 6 months · 6 months or more · It wouldn't be needed

screens.why1: Right after I said how long the data protection review would take, it is obvious why they ask what would hold the purchase up.
screens.why2: I understand it on first reading and can answer in my own words: the data protection officer, the works council, the contract with the hotels.
screens.why3: I have bought booking and telephony tools for the group, so I know which steps drag and who holds them up.
screens.why4: A box to type in, with no options or chips to judge.
screens.why5: It uses only the name Codyco from the idea card already shown, and no founder terms or roles reach me beyond that.
screens.why6: One short question that says easily and can be answered after one hearing; the bundle records no spoken form for it, so this is judged on the template's reading.

screens.why1: After the price, the budget, the sign-off and the data protection review, it is obvious why the study now asks whether I would actually pay for a pilot at one hotel.
screens.why2: Pilot, one hotel and €3,000 are everyday words in my job, so I can answer on first reading, even though I would want to know what triggers the money-back.
screens.why3: I decide on and pay for tools like this, and €3,000 for a pilot at one hotel is the low end of the up-front range I gave, so I can answer from my own budget and authority.
screens.why4: The three options cover the answer, but there is a firm yes and two kinds of no with no leaning-yes option, so my real answer of yes if the data protection review clears gets pushed into Probably not, which sits close to No.
screens.why5: The idea card is shown on purpose and the question uses only the idea's name and a plain pilot offer, with no founder's terms or roles reaching me.
screens.why6: It is one short balanced question with three short options I can hold after one hearing, and three thousand euros says easily.
screens.instead: If it were ready today, would you pay €3,000 for a money-back pilot at one hotel, or not? Yes · Probably yes · Probably not · No
